items.title: Rocket Fuel Math
items.question: ISRO's cryogenic rocket engine burns liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen. If a rocket burns 1500 kg of liquid hydrogen (LH2) and 7500 kg of liquid oxygen (LOX), what is the total mass of the propellants burnt?
items.explanation: Add the mass of the fuel and the oxidizer together: 1500 kg + 7500 kg = 9000 kg.

items.title: The Cosmic Thief
items.question: I have no body, but I can steal your breath. I have no mouth, but I can steal your oxygen. I have no legs, but I can pull you into my darkness. What am I?
items.explanation: A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. It 'steals' light and matter (and by extension, oxygen/breath) by pulling it into its event horizon, which is its 'darkness'.

items.title: Chandrayaan-3
items.passage: In August 2023, ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 mission landed its Vikram lander near the south pole of the Moon. No country had ever landed there before! Scientists are curious about this area because some of its craters may hold frozen water.
items.question: What was special about where Chandrayaan-3 landed?
options: It was the first landing near the Moon's south pole
It was the first landing on Mars
It landed in the middle of the ocean
items.answer: It was the first landing near the Moon's south pole
items.explanation: India became the first country ever to land near the Moon's south pole, where there may be frozen water.

items.title: Rocket Fuel
items.question: A rocket needs 2,500 kg of fuel to take off. It burns 800 kg of fuel in the first stage, 750 kg in the second stage, and 450 kg in the third stage. How much fuel is left for the final landing?
items.explanation: Subtract the stages: 800 + 750 + 450 = 2000. Subtract from total: 2500 - 2000 = 500 kg.

items.title: The Astronaut's Dilemma
items.question: An astronaut is floating in space with a broken spacesuit. He has a flashlight, a rope, and a bottle of water. He needs to get back to his spaceship, which is 100 meters away. How can he get back?
options: He throws the bottle of water in the opposite direction to propel himself forward.
He shines the flashlight to create a beam of light that pushes him forward.
He ties the rope to his suit and pulls himself forward.
He waits for the spaceship to move closer to him.
items.answer: He throws the bottle of water in the opposite direction to propel himself forward.
items.explanation: By Newton's third law of motion, throwing the water in one direction creates an equal and opposite reaction, pushing the astronaut toward the spaceship.

items.title: Why Does the Ball Swing?
items.passage: Fast bowlers rub one side of the cricket ball on their trousers to keep it shiny. Air slides smoothly over the shiny side but gets bumpy and messy on the rough side. This difference pushes the ball sideways in the air, and that curve is called swing!
items.question: Why do bowlers keep one side of the ball shiny?
options: So air flows differently on each side and the ball swings
So the ball looks nice on TV
So the batter cannot see the ball
items.answer: So air flows differently on each side and the ball swings
items.explanation: The shiny side and rough side make air flow differently, which pushes the ball sideways.

items.title: Monsoon Savings
items.question: Rahul saves ₹10 every day during the 30 days of July to buy a new cricket bat. How much money does he save in total?
items.explanation: Multiply 10 by 30, which equals 300 rupees.

items.title: Mission Control Grid
items.question: Each row of this grid follows the same rule.  Row 1: 3, 5, 8.  Row 2: 4, 6, 10.  Row 3: 7, 2, ?  What is the missing number?
items.explanation: In every row, the first number plus the second number gives the third. 7 + 2 = 9!

items.title: The Monsoon's Umbrella
items.question: I have a tongue but cannot talk. I wear a coat but have no body. I live in the monsoon and love to hide in the earth. What am I?
items.explanation: Earthworms come out during the monsoon to avoid drowning in waterlogged soil. They are known to have a 'tongue-like' structure (prostomium) and are often called 'earth's intestines' or 'nature's plough'.

items.title: Where Does the Monsoon Come From?
items.passage: In summer, the land in India heats up much faster than the ocean. Hot air over the land rises up, and cool, wet wind from the Indian Ocean rushes in to take its place. That wet wind carries clouds full of water, and that is the monsoon!
items.question: What brings monsoon rain to India?
options: Wet winds blowing in from the ocean
Water rising from rivers at night
Clouds made by trains and cars
items.answer: Wet winds blowing in from the ocean
items.explanation: Hot land pulls in wet ocean wind, and that wind drops its water as monsoon rain.

items.title: The Run Rate
items.question: In an IPL match, Team India scored 150 runs in the first 10 overs. What is their required run rate in runs per over?
items.explanation: To find the run rate, divide the total runs by the total overs: 150 ÷ 10 = 15 runs per over.

items.title: Who Has the Banana?
items.question: Asha, Bilal and Chitra each have one different fruit: a mango, a banana or a guava. Asha does not have the banana or the guava. Bilal does not have the banana. Who has the banana?
items.explanation: Asha must have the mango. Bilal can't have the banana, so he has the guava. That leaves the banana for Chitra!

items.title: Keys Without Locks
items.question: I have lots of keys, but I can't open a single lock. What am I?
items.explanation: A piano has black and white keys that make music, not keys that open locks!

items.title: Colours in the Sky

items.question: What gives fireworks their different colours?
options: The colour of the night sky
items.explanation: Each metal glows a special colour when it gets very hot, like copper glowing blue.

items.question: In a T20 match, Team A scored 24 runs in the first 3 overs. What is their required run rate per over?
items.explanation: Divide the total runs by the number of overs: 24 runs ÷ 3 overs = 8 runs per over.

items.title: Platform Dash
items.question: A train is 400 metres long and travels at a speed of 60 km/h. How many seconds does it take to completely cross a 200-metre-long platform?
items.explanation: First, add the train's length and the platform's length: 400 m + 200 m = 600 m. Then, convert the speed from km/h to m/s: 60 × (5/18) = 50/3 m/s. Finally, divide the total distance by the speed: 600 ÷ (50/3) = 600 × (3/50) = 36 seconds.
